DESCRIPTION: There is an element of steel to the character of a greater sabre-toothed cat. Fierce, strong, independent, vigilant, and spiritual.
You'd expect that eastern long-necked turtles would live in the east, but years ago all fled to the west when their homeland was sacked.
Lesser white-toothed shrews are infamous storytellers and braggers. To them, truth is in the eye of the beholder.
There is an element of steel to the character of a greater sabre-toothed cat. Fierce, strong, independent, vigilant, and spiritual.
A real danger for black-tailed prairie dogs is becoming obsessed with their goals. It can vex them into mental breakdowns.
Named after their obvious feature, scarlet-headed blackbirds moan about how many outfits clash with their feathers.
When one wants to be stylish, the vain but enviable golden-fronted bowerbirds are the ones to ask guidance from.
Despite being named African helmeted turtles, they usually don't like wearing anything on their head.
Something always worries black-tailed jackrabbits. As such, they go to great lengths to manage their stress.
Because of how old and scruffy grizzled giant squirrels look, they invest in beauty product to look younger.
Often called 'the late', Chiriqui harlequin frogs are fading from the world. In a few years, they may not be here any longer.
Saddled with the colour blue, Tenerife blue chaffinches go to great lengths working different shades of blue in what they wear.
Aldabra giant tortoises are massive islanders who make some of the wisest, if slowest, sailors.
When staying still, the stump-tailed chameleon can imitate dead plants. A power it uses to hide from foes and in-laws.
The diurnal yellow-throated toucans originate from a tropical island chain, where they style themselves as vassals of a sun god.
Blue-winged kookaburras have piercing pale eyes, which they use to intimidate discounts and favours out of others.
Prepared is the single best word to describe grizzled tree-kangaroos. For their homeland is beset by enemies on all sides.
All long-nosed horned frogs, regardless of the culture they come from, are drawn to esoteric traditions from distant lands.
Long-tailed chinchillas follow strict matriarchal social structures and rarely fight among themselves.
Only male three-horned chameleons have horns, which they flaunt to their rivals to show how 'powerful' they are.
Flat-headed rock agamas are great at sneaking, but terrible at making friends. They usually prefer to live in solitude.
Strawberry poison frogs get easily attached to others, hoping to make trustworthy life-long friends to enjoy the world with.
An old tale claims that Asian forest tortoises of the east live in houses mounted on massive trees. Claims these scalefolks deny.
The larger Eurasian capercaillies have trouble living in cities. When older, they leave their lives to start anew in the woods.
It takes years of work for a nine-banded armadillo to be satisfied with something they've made. Picky, in a word.
European wall lizards have a motto, 'In hard times, hang on harder'. They apply this to all of life's woes.
No conversation can be discreet while a brown long-eared bat is around. They don't mean to listen in, but can't help it.
Great eared nightjars are an eastern nocturnal bird. They are of the mindset that nightwork is preferable to more traditional hours.
Orange-bellied macaws once held an old empire in South America, but were defeated and driven out by scarlet macaws.
The world's newest taboos and odd fads are attempted by pink hair armadillos. They like to indulge in peculiar behaviours.
A recent children's book put out by Boriwe Publishing playfully states rusty-spotted cats colour their fur by rolling in autumn leaves.
Pinta giant tortoises have a tendency to immerse themselves in one field, getting stuck for decades, centuries even.
While not quite as polite as others of their kin, giant burrowing frogs are still always ready to offer their help. For a cost.
Folks are vary of Long-winged tomb bats. A portion of them taking part in stealthy illegal activies taints them all.
Pressured by their heritage, northern banded newt youth tend to be highly educated but also timid and wary of change.
You should be scared if a sabre-toothed cat holds you in fierce stare. They like striking fast and hard in combat and business.
What short-beaked echidnas call 'sharing', other folks call 'taking my stuff and leaving something random in its place'.
With their eye-catching plumage, white-cheeked turacos take pride in their looks, no matter where or when you meet one.
When troubled by the present, Madagascar day geckos linger on the past and go on about how much better it was.
The American black bear is imposing, but glad just to live a small, quiet life without much in the way of drama or ambition.
Entry to be added a bit later.
Siberian salamanders are the best equipped palefolk to live in cold environments, even able to survive in arctic conditions.
Black-footed ferrets find it enchanting to just move into other folk's homes and live with them. With or without permission.
The only thing great about great crested grebes is their ability to over-reach and make outlandishly dumb excuses for their failures.
Famous for being able to show you their spine through their mouth, great white pelicans enjoy grossing others out.
Red-crested pochards strive to differentiate themselves from other duck species and boast about how they are the best divers.
Not much matches the wicked wit of a rhinoceros hornbill, except for the strange upwards curvature of its casque.
Slender-billed gulls have short sleek beaks as black as the night. Poems attribute this to gulls attempting to swallow the sun.
The best sun-bathing spots are often hogged by spiny-tailed lizards, if they aren't off in their underground clubs.
Folk feel uncomfortable under the stern gaze of a black-collared hawk. The best their mood can get is 'smouldering'.
Pale-throated sloths make diligent workers, always following orders given. Just don't expect them to be swift.
For viciously attacking trees and topped with a flaming red crest, pileated woodpeckers were thought to be in league with fire spirits.
Gold dust day geckos have adventurous urges to go out and explore all day long, stopping to help those in need.
Due to sickness and wildfires, American alligators once faced extinction. Now they have swelled in numbers.
Beach stone-curlews enjoy activities that don't require you to be close to others. Their large beaks get caught on everything.
You'd be hard-pressed to find a sport that isn't attended by athletic and excitable emerald tree skinks in droves.
Giant ground sloths are nearly a myth. Monsters in size and strength, many live in isolation on a distant and uncharted island.
It has been a long-standing tradition for keel-billed toucans to pierce their beaks, which they deem as a sign of toughness.
The extended throat of a long-necked turtle allows them to indulge in their nosey behaviour of putting their snouts where they don't belong.
Red-breasted geese like to be wherever trouble and danger is at. Something about 'being closer to it means we're safer'.
When something doesn't need to be changed, you can bet a rough-tailed gecko complicates it with their 'daring ideas'.
Young thick-billed murres are harshly tested by their parents, making them self-reliant and sympathetic to those struggling.
With the largest wingspan of any eagle, white-tailed eagles are seen as 'heroic' and 'larger than life' by other avians.
For the longest time, yellow-legged gulls haven't been officially recognised until recently, making them proud and independent.
So sturdy and indestructible, other folks get anxious seeing greater guinea pigs being test subjects in crazy experiments.
Foul-mouthed torrent salamanders enjoy the cold. They see activities in cold water as the best way to spend one's free time.
The most striking feature of the blue-tongued skink, besides the striking colour of their mouth, is their unstable minds.
When a glance at their intense and clashing colours can cause dizziness and nausea, red-eyed tree frogs dress heavily.
Red-necked wallaby parents are in a world of hurt, their young being extremely headstrong and fast, never lacking energy.
If there is one breed that is forever in discontent, it is the white-headed lemurs. Nothing holds their interest for long.
A famous tale tells of a Siberian chipmunk squeezing her home city's entire population into her cheeks, rescuing them from a flood.
Swift of foot and stocky, cottontail rabbits have an unconscious urge to forage, even in this day and age.
An urge to hunt possesses red-footed falcons with no care for themselves. When they are set to a task, they will die in pursuit.
Ring-tailed lemurs wear their tails about their necks as scarfs, boasting of the care given to their attached fashion accessory.
A recent children's book put out by Boriwe Publishing playfully states rusty-spotted cats colour their fur by rolling in autumn leaves.
White-tailed moles are on the smaller side of the mole family, but are viewed as 'lucky' by other burrowing folks for reasons unknown.
The European hedgehog is well known for being prickly. Not just in their literal spikes, but also in their personality.
Thanks to their lavish yellow brows, Fiordland penguins appear wiser than they generally are. Something they never admit.
No deal is off limits, no good classified as junk. Swindling black-headed gulls are both loved and hated trading partners.
Panther chameleons in the past adapted to their physical environments to survive. Now they do so in the social and political.
You should be scared if a sabre-toothed cat holds you in fierce stare. They like striking fast and hard in combat and business.
The striking features of white-headed ducks are singular. Their colours, as the ducks claim, represent their rich culture.
Wreathed hornbills are so fixated on their large bills that they often go to spas to get them manicured.
Yellow-tailed rats have tails longer than other rodents, and use that as a measurement of one's treachery.

Eurasian polecats are just as courageous as other polecats, but are also known by the cruelly as 'foul martens' for their strong odour.
You'd think that European hamsters would be timid for their size, but in reality they are very aggressive and defiant.
Well-adjusted to living at higher altitudes, dusky salamanders settle on any career that involves going into mountain wilderness.
Though their stripes are fetching, five-lined skinks regard their patterns to be ugly birthmarks, for some silly reason.
With their territorial nature and lust for devouring fish, giant kingfishers like to work security gigs near bodies of water.
The large great horned owl is adaptable to many situations, and prone to trying to solve their problems by themselves.
With such long necks, greater flamingos see it as both a blessing and a curse – one they endure with grace and pride.
Queues and crowds are the bane of long-tailed ducks. They memorise each time someone has stepped on their tail.
Ocellated lizards of old were both predators and prey. From this, they swing between timid and bullies.
There might not be any visually or vocally louder bird than the rainbow lorikeet. So they do their best to go unnoticed.
European polecats are less reckless than other polecats, but have an air of authority, making them natural leadership material.
With the power to critically harm others with a touch, blue poison dart frogs try to keep their digits to themselves.
Feathers of blue, white, and orange cover the striking river kingfishers. In two words, they're territorial and sharp-eye'd.
Lively slender mongooses drive themselves to work at break-neck speeds. When not heartbroken by social drama.
The desert rain frog is emotional and well-learned. Their squeaky voice, however, makes everything they say sound like a joke.
Thieving isn't all northern raccoons, a folk without a land to call their own, do. They also smuggle and counterfeit, among other things.
Some living up to 400 years, veiled chameleons are like living history books. Ones that only open up to their closest friends.
With jet black and metallic green feathers, Eurasian magpies think they look 'wicked sick' and 'rad'.
Growing up to immense sizes, boa constrictors wrap around their prey and crush them before swallowing them whole.
Looking goofy, collared lizards can run very fast standing straight up. Something they fall back on when their schemes fail.
Old scrolls claimed that the spiritual emperor tamarins lived in heavenly palaces and mastered both spirits and elements.
It seems every griffon vulture knows the story of how their kin were once monstrous world-conquering birds, brought low by the god Tam.
Mongrel dogs are a fusion between two different types of parents. There is no limit to what shape or size they can be.
The bard lifestyle has absorbed more purple starlings than any other species. They have strong singing voices and egos.
Every so often, hospitals have to treat red-tailed hawks who have injured themselves during ariel stunts, trying to impress others.
Possessing strange tendril noses and massive claws, star-nosed moles were believed to be monsters by early historians.
Systematic to a fault, Eurasian beavers have guidelines and rules in place for nearly everything one could ever think of.
The mischeavous Tasmanian devils keep those in power on their toes. Someone growing contented is a sign of revolution.
Bearded vultures have strong family ties to one another, and live by an ancient set of laws their ancestors made.
While individual dwarf crocodiles can be intimidating, wait until you meet a mafia group led by one. You don't want that.
The vigorous emperor penguins form tighter communities than others. A trait stemming from their harsh living environment.
What others see as junk to throw away, the flying squirrel hoards like its life depends on it. They truly believe it does.
Maybe the most reckless of all polecats, marbled polecats seek adventure wherever and whenever. With unyielding resolve.
From the country of Olicam, spectacled bears are honourable and stalwart. Unless they are angered. Then the bets are off.
There are entire news organisations run by Atlantic puffins, with the high goal of publishing the most unbiased of reports.
Unlike its family members, the Eurasian badger is highly empathetic. They get sad whey they to get mixed with their cousins.
Rarely staying at one place for long, Eurasian hoopoes make great travelling companions, always ready for the next 'thing'.
Little in this world can survive the crushing bite of a snapping turtle. A feat these grumpy folks are ever eager to show off.
Once named for their obsession with flames, fire salamanders burn long and bright with fervour to achieve greatness.
Most of the year, Eurasian cranes watch what they eat, as during the summer they are struck by gratuitous appetites.
Eurasian otters are committed to the arts of fur styling and cloth-dying. This passion of theirs doubles as a source of income.
Old tales claim that Indian peafowls were created by a trickster entity known as the Great Liar, when mocked over a claim.
It is said that the first bearded dragon swallowed a thorn branch to give her descendants protective spikes.
Entry to be added a bit later.
Also known as the 'jumping shrews', elephant shrews can leap into the air several times the height of their own body.
Some of the longest living animalfolk, giant tortoises, and the memories they carry can act as a window to the past.
While mountain sheep are significantly stronger than their cousins, their fiery temper is not something to be underestimated.
While not many would know of it, or even think of it, naked mole-rats are serious athletes who compete in underground games.
One thing Daimyria's animalfolks can't resist is making oriental tapirs into their pets and making them wear cute hats.
Avians who hunted other animals in the past are called birds of prey. They have progressed past this, but still have hungry eyes.
Pygmy marmosets are obsessed with grooming others and cleaning everything they see. They make great roommates.
When two sandhill cranes meet for the first time, they sing to each other to judge how much they like the other.
Secretary birds are tall, tough-legged, snake eaters. In their homelands, they solve disputes with lightning-fast kicking matches.
Siberian huskies come from a once-great empire in the north. They left their decaying home to live and work elsewhere.
Burrowing frogs are the kind of folk that wouldn't let you sit in their comfy personal hole, but they will help dig one for you.
Resisting the migration urges of their kin, gentoo penguins strive to 'sink their roots deep' in their local communities.
Giant pangolins have a fickle personality and over-all posture. Their absent-mindedness is only a part of the equation.
Steppe polecats are the second most common polecat breed of Galzyr's most numerous species. Like its kin, they are aggressive and hardy.
Archiving data is in desert monitors' cold blood. The largest known collection of information gathered during centuries.
The boasty nature of frilled lizards is only compounded by their ability to appear larger by opening their majestic frills.
A giant anteater can't resist wandering into folk's yards and digging up their gardens looking for a snack.
Stories of old tell red salamanders to be ancient forest guardians. A legacy they carry proudly still today.
Some clay tablets state that the first blue chaffinches guarded dragon trees against the trickster god known as the Great Liar.
Eurasian teals, with their widely varied diet that changes between the seasons, consider themselves to be gourmands.
Ignorant of personal space, European minks like to get up close to other folks and ask about anything that comes to mind.
The wild bobcat plays with others and their possessions without care. They don't mean to hurt or break anything, but often do.
Other avians feel that burrowing owls should have been mammals. What kind of bird likes digging and playing in the mud?
Golden jackals yearn to be in the open vastness of the desert. They'd rather tread on burning sand than sleep in a comfy bed.
Once a humble seafaring folk, many great bustards have dipped their feet in piracy or naval enlistment.
Being the largest of the squirrels, grumpy grey squirrels take on the role of being an older sibling to all other squirrels.
Greyleg gooses aren't often moved or impressed by much, but when they are, they can get a little giddy about it.
Horned lizards still posses an odd trait from their primitive ancestors, the ability to squirt blood from their eyes.
The self-important howler monkey is said to posses the loudest voice of all folk. Its howl can be heard kilometres away.
If nothing else, mountain hares are timid but polite. Their northern home is filled with frights that shaped them to be this way.
Some restaurants keep pine cones on hand in case ravenous but fussy pine squirrels decide to come eat.
Known as 'nature's fool', piping plovers are forgetful and easily persuaded, but seem to always get their work done right.
Everyone claims spider monkeys to be devious troublemakers. To such an extreme, that the Great Liar is accused of creating them.
Not many animalfolks in Daimyria recall that striped skunks can spray a foul musk, as they strike to subdue such behaviour.
Stern, hard-working, and unfaltering in their course, European moles are sought after in the workforce.
Legends state that alpine marmots can have snow-white fur if they spend years living and meditating in high altitudes.
It's easy to find bat-eared foxes cute. They have the most adorable little faces, and always try their hardest to please others.
Silent, powerful, and greedy, black panthers often find themselves in bodyguard jobs, knowing how possible threats act.
You'd be hard-pressed to find a better shoot than a leopard gecko. They have sharp eyes and enjoy showing off their dexterity.
While little weasels are the smallest of weasel-kind, they have extreme personalities and a taste for trickery beyond that of their larger kin.
A strong sense of justice defines the lives of mandarin ducks. They devote their lives to their partners and working lives.
The pointed hooves of the mountain goat allow it to scale insane surfaces and reach the most dangerous of places.
Hailing from an empire in South America, the vibrant and snappy scarlet macaws have made tantrum-throwing an art form.
There aren't many things the superstitious snowshoe hares don't believe in. Nothing seems too farfetched or weird to them.
Hyenas are rare across Daimyria, the striped hyena being the least studied. They are often mixed up with other hyenas.
Vervet monkeys have no qualms about using the homes of others for their jungle-gyms, and have no respect for infrastructure.
Eurasian lynxes have natural urges to travel far and wide, unbothered by crossing distances on foot that would break others.
Komodo dragons are thick-framed, muscular, tough, and possess a deadly bite. No surprise they are desirable for war.
Rainbow agamas have such vibrant and striking scale colours that they are considered living works of art.
Adapted for arboreal locomotion, tree-kangaroos would prefer to climb up trees to their higher destinations instead of taking the stairs.
Neighbours groan when a local Asian badger starts digging in the middle of the night. They make up for it in community cookouts.

Most beach martens vacation in the spring, so they can spend each night going for swims in the cold ocean during warm nights.
Avians who hunted other animals in the past are called birds of prey. They have progressed past this, but still have hungry eyes.
Contrary to their kin, not many bobak marmots have strong desire to seek spiritual enlightenment. Earthly riches suffice.
Each forest in the world has a good chance of containing a secret capercaillie colony. These forest folks enjoy their privacy.
Modern carrion crows are unsure why they have been given this name. Eating the dead is icky! They hope to be renamed soon.
All cave swallows in a city will live together in the closest and most cramped conditions possible, even if they don't know each other.
Eastern newts are excellent swimmers thanks to their slick, pale skin combined with their slender silhouette.
Golden eagles try to be humble, as a newer myth states they were chosen by a golden comet to one day rule the world.
Vicious and protective of their family, grizzly bears will commit any taboo or break any laws needed to keep their family safe.
Herring gulls have become learned in spices and cooking to better flavour all the trash and rubbish they devour.
The staunchly ignorant honey badger just doesn't care about others. Got a problem with that? They'll fight you over it.
Rock monitors are known for holding their ground, being heavy, slow-paced creatures that refuse to back down.
Long legs and bright golden eyes that are always moving, stone-curlews look like they're constantly searching for something.
Many athletic areas have elevated platforms where sugar gliders can carry out their games of catching moths mid-air.
The mouth of the scaled Gila monster is filled with venom and kind words for anyone they cross. Just nice folks they are.
With their skills in climbing, swimming, and jumping, green iguanas scale over any obstacle to get to where they want.
It amazes many that red-kangaroos are lazy and non-responsive, but settle every argument with a boxing match.
With red squirrels coming in so many fur colours other than red, they just accept all squirrels as part of their family.
Snow leopards are experts in winter conditions and love the study of military history, making snowball fights a sacred sport to them.
In lands far east of Gemsed, steppe mice have built a dozenscore of earth-mound cities as a foundation for a new country.
The spine covered skin of thorny devils complicates their ability to hug others, but grants marvellous protection against attackers.
One of the cutest animalfolks in Daimyria is the white cuscus. More often than not, they're off in their own little world.
What others classify as scheming, green magpies simply attribute to serving their god Tam, for the betterment of all Daimyria.
There is a string of temples in the north-east depicting Burmese cats fighting with wavering blades. No one knows why.
As morbid fish-catchers and vicious fighters, black storks hold a grim and underserved reputation as unfeeling assassins.
Bulldog rats are the kind of folks who would like to do everything discreetly and under the table, as long as no one gets hurt.
Across Daimyria, the term marinefolk, or flipperfolk, covers those that have flippers and struggle to move on land.
It is credited that the frigatebird got its huge red throat when their first generation swallowed hearts of the foes they felled.
Almost three times larger than other otters, giant otters are seen by their peers as 'big protective siblings' of their aquatic communities.
Many grey marmots are textbook bullies. They walk all over and exploit those smaller than them, but cower at real power.
Hooded crows seemingly give 'random' folks gold and gifts. Really, it's to repay all the food they've secretly taken from them.
Hummingbirds know nothing of pacing themselves. Everything they do, talk, eat, work, is done in a careless rush.
Many folks find it eerie how mockingbirds can replicate sounds and voices. Years ago, others believed they were mimics.
Mongrel dogs are a fusion between two different types of parents. There is no limit to what shape or size they can be.
Prairie dogs fear for the end and stockpile supplies. They think their own shadows act as hand on a clock for the countdown.
The pointy snout of a purple frog is a source of pride for them. Individuals with long noses are both looked up to and envied.
River Otters live in small little mobile villages that they move up and down rivers through the different seasons.
All sand lizards see themselves as tiny-bodied but big-hearted, defenders of nature. At least while they are not vacationing at resorts.
Sloth lemurs are a dying race, so they work to build up their numbers and seek more places to build secret communes.
These clever furfolk love taking hot baths. As such, snow monkeys in Galzyr are usually found at Chabahr's hot springs.
With advancements to structural engineering, wall lizards have more and more vertical surfaces to climb wherever they go.
Native to South America, agami herons value cultural preservation and have an unending thirst for knowledge.
Crocodilians is a crocodile-like group of semiaquatic scalefolks. Many of which are large, armoured, and great at parties.
The most defining trait of featherfolks, or birds, is their ability to fly. Something even their flightless individuals envy.
As preservers of fading cultural lore, field mice have a strong sense of traditions and oppose the values of the Great Liar.
For giant pandas, dealing is a way of life. Everything is for sale, and everyone benefits from putting a good deal down in black and white.
With a near limitless vocal repertoire, nightingales shine in communication, be it acting, politics, or simply being really loud.
And old joke is that silver fish were born from silver coins that 'rotted' when tight-fisted owners didn't spend them.
Monstrous in size, many of the aptly named terror birds sell their services either as combatants or beasts of burden.
Not many can guess a more intelligent connection beyond the name, but tiger geckos are obsessed with wearing tiger pattern clothes.
The largest of their family, toco toucans have a colourful beak, weighing a third of their mass. Used to impress, and to defend.
Zebra finches age fastest of any birds. Their young adults petition for many age restrictions to be lowered for them.
The agilisaurus should be designated as the true 'party animals'. To them, no celebration should be either cheap, small, or short.
An ancient legend tells banded newts being mythical creatures, born from raindrops and destined to rule the seas.
Horned frogs have weaker and shorter limbs than other palefolk. Despite this, they focus on cultivating a stronger spirit.
A single, unprotected touch of a poison frog can put you in the hospital. So these frogs are careful in who and what they touch.
Bold in numbers but cautious alone, timber wolves feel a need to establish dominance. Preferably, with themselves on top.
The shelled reptile known as the wood turtle is driven by an enthusiastic need to create artistic works.
The artsy fairy prion enjoys criticising others work more than creating any themselves. A habit not many are fond of.

Talkative Asian toads are known for their youth gathering in extremely large groups when they socialise.
Adult Bengal cats keep their child-like playfulness and strong-willed nature. Unlike other cats, they also don't mind water.
The black bear may seem scary, but really they are the ones who are afraid of everyone else. So don't bully them please!
Boreal owls enjoy the cold more than the rest of the owls do and take a keen interest in winter sports and building snowfolk.
It is in the nature of chuckwallas to live on a coast and raise walls. Why? They don't know. They just like islands and walls.
Swift of foot and stocky, cottontail rabbits have an unconscious urge to forage, even in this day and age.
Grey herons hunger for learning and moulding their own culture to that of past civilisations now extinct.
Jackrabbits are very nervous about going outdoors and prefer attending low-energy underground parties.
Across Daimyria, the term marinefolk, or flipperfolk, covers those that have flippers and struggle to move on land.
It is said that mossy frogs were the pray of a mythical hunting bird, so they begged the spirits of the earth to camouflage their skin.
Mouse-deers are the smallest and most timid of any kind of deer, and are unable to grow horns or antlers.
Both tunnelling folk and flying birds think pink robins, who have no affinity for digging, are crazy for wanting to live underground.
Entry to be added a bit later.
Never put your guard down around sloth bears. It takes a tiny inconvenience for them to snap and get absurdly violent.
Animalfolks are the dominant beings of Daimyria, all with their own beliefs, varied communities, and interconnected civilisations.
There is no trail a bloodhound won't, or can't follow. To them, there is an intoxicating purpose to find absolute closure.
Brown bears usually care more about ideas and theories than they do about wealth or items. A foreign concept to the greedy.
Research shows that chimpanzees were the first folk to use tools. Greatly skilled with items, they also have violent streaks.
Some seafood restaurants swear they are kept in business only by voracious and generous kingfisher customers.
While as wise as any other owl, little owls are usually not given the same reputation as they are shy and rarely speak.
Polar bears are massive carnivores with appetites to match their size. Thankfully, they no longer hunt other folks these days.
Legends claim that salamanders were born from fire. Though these palefolks hold no obvious protection against heat.
Wide-eyed and considered cute by all, many slow loris are treated as kids, much to their adorable ire.
The most calm a snow goose can be is 'ecstatic', or maybe even 'hyper'. Unlike the lifeless, grey lands they hail from.
Hailing from the south-east, sphynxes were once treated as gods and buried in great tombs alongside their possessions.
Not only do Arctic foxes find talent where others don't, they're also masters at making folk reach their maximum potential.
The tiny chinchilla may look cute and cuddly, but when stressed, their personality randomly warps, and they become unhinged.
Friendly, sly, and cute. Fennec foxes always seem to get what they want, especially when interacting with strangers.
Guinea pigs are mechanically-minded and enjoy inventing. Just that the only inventions they like are ones for racing.
All hairy frogs love to salvage and re-use stuff, but males can break their finger bones to make claws 'grow' out of their tips.
Kookaburras have loud, zany laughs and seem to cackle at everything and everyone as if they were comedy gold.
Islanders by nature, warrah foxes take to the seafaring life. Their menacing look hides their softer nature.
Woodpeckers are perfectionists and woodworkers, unapproving of clients who lack the patience to wait for their finished products.

The harmonious Inca doves are building an earthly palace for the goddess Ito. A desire gifted to them by the deity herself.
Thanks to their unique structure, armadillos can curl into a ball and roll away, escaping arguments they don't want to have.
The grumpy binturong is used to multitasking, using their prehensile tail to hold stuff when they don't have a free paw available.
Coveting anything sweet, fruit bats are ready to trade almost anything for an exotic fruit they haven't tasted yet. Almost.
Great auks romanticise the opinion that one's life doesn't matter. A dark virtue they preach with little pride in their delivery.
